title: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)
hook: a hunter caught in a storm shelters under the tree where he just trapped a pigeon, and her mate decides he is a guest
carry: the hunter laid down his nets

segments.voice: Yesterday in Shanti and Anushasana, a starving sage stole forbidden food, and the man he stole from defended dharma. Your line was a dead sage helps no one. Did you catch yourself calling something an emergency? Today, another of Bhishma's stories. Day eight hundred sixty-four.
screen: `SHANTI AND ANUSHASANA.` · `WHEN THE RULES RUN OUT.`

segments.voice: A storm breaks over the forest. A hunter, a hard man who lives by trapping birds, is caught out in it, soaked and shaking with cold. In his cage is a female pigeon he caught that day. He stumbles to a big tree and crouches under it for shelter. He doesn't know that the tree is her home. Up in its branches her mate is grieving, wondering where she's gone. And from inside the cage, she can hear him. Yudhishthira had asked Bhishma about a person who gives shelter to someone who comes asking for it. This is the story Bhishma tells. Today, the pigeons and the hunter.
screen: `A STORM IN THE FOREST.` → `A HUNTER UNDER THEIR TREE.` → `SHE HEARS HER MATE.`

segments.voice: The female pigeon calls up to her mate, and what she says is startling. Don't grieve for me, she tells him. This man has come to our home, cold and hungry. He's our guest. Treat him as one. And the male pigeon does. He fetches a burning ember from somewhere and gathers dry leaves, and he makes a fire so the hunter can warm himself. Then he realizes he has nothing to feed his guest. He has no store of grain, nothing set aside. So he does the only thing he can think of. He offers himself, and drops into the fire, so the hunter will have food. The hunter is undone. The man who caught birds for a living has just watched a bird give its life to feed him. He opens the cage and lets the female go. But she, grieving her mate, follows him into the fire too. And the story says the two of them rise to heaven together, shining. The hunter can't go back to who he was. He throws away his nets and his cage, gives up hunting, and goes off into the forest to live in austerity. The word underneath all of this is atithi, the guest. In the dharma Bhishma teaches, a guest who comes to your door is to be honored, whoever they are, even an enemy, even the person who hurt you. It's an extreme story, and the text tells it as extreme. Bhishma isn't asking the new king to leap into fires. He's showing him how far hospitality reaches: past fairness, past safety, all the way to the person who did you harm.
screen: `"HE IS OUR GUEST"` · `A FIRE FOR THE HUNTER` · `THE PIGEON GIVES HIMSELF` · then, large: `THE HUNTER LAYS DOWN HIS NETS`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your hands rest open. Bring to mind someone who will come through your door, or your inbox, or your day, who isn't easy to welcome. Breathe in, and see them arriving. Breathe out, and in your mind offer them something small: warmth, a seat, a glass of water, your full attention. Nothing heroic. Just one real welcome. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
atithi. Guest: the one who comes to your door, to be honored, whoever they are, even the person who hurt you.
Your line: the hunter laid down his nets. Today, give one person a welcome they didn't expect. Tomorrow, a snake, a grieving mother, Death and Time. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu teaching treats the guest, atithi, as someone to be honored, and a line from the Taittiriya Upanishad, 'atithi devo bhava', let the guest be as a god, names the same ideal; Bhishma's story of the pigeons is retold as an illustration.

fork.setup: you're the male pigeon. the man who trapped your mate is shivering under your tree, and she says he's your guest. what do you do?
options: fly away and leave him to the storm.
make him a fire, and give him what food you have.
wait for him to sleep and free your mate.
fork.reveal: he makes a fire, and having no food, gives himself; the hunter, undone, frees the female and gives up hunting.

original.note: guest: one who comes to your door, to be honored whoever they are.

trapdoor: what you thought: the pigeons are a sad animal fable.
what it means: they're Bhishma's picture of hospitality, honoring even the one who harmed you.
what a scholar hears: the story sits in Bhishma's teaching on dharma in distress, and it turns a hunter's cruelty into renunciation through a guest-offering.
